detail.title: England-wide injury-severity analysis of e-scooter riders using a Bayesian spatial field model
detail.abstract: The rising popularity of electric scooters (e-scooters) has led to increased crashes, posing significant road safety challenges. This study analyses 2,128 crashes involving e-scooters and motor vehicles across England (2020-2023) to identify factors associated with severe injuries to e-scooter riders. Using the geographic coordinates of crashes, we developed a Bayesian spatial field model implemented via the Stochastic Partial Differential Equation approach for fast Bayesian estimation. Our approach accounts for spatial unobserved heterogeneity often overlooked in injury severity studies, improving model fit substantially. We demonstrate the ease with which spatially varying coefficients can be incorporated into the analysis, even in a computationally intensive setting. Results indicate that severe or fatal injuries are more likely among older riders, male riders, and in crashes occurring in darkness, on single carriageways, on roads with speed limits of 40 mph or higher, involving heavy vehicles, at night or early morning, or with e-scooter skidding/overturning, frontal impacts, e-scooters entering main roads, or opponent vehicles moving straight. Conversely, motor vehicles performing moving-off manoeuvres are linked to lower odds of severe injuries. Our spatial analysis revealed that in parts of northwestern and southeastern England, e-scooter riders exhibit higher odds of severe injury compared with the national average. These findings inform evidence-based policies to enhance e-scooter safety in England and elsewhere.

title: Information and Misinformation in Networks
affiliations: Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata - Economic Research Unit and Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata

detail.title: Information and Misinformation in Networks
detail.abstract: We study a non-cooperative game in which agents are connected in a (exogenously given) social network and there exists uncertainty captured through states of the world. Each agent receives a private (partial) signal about the true state of the world. They then pass messages privately (truthfully or misreporting) to their neighbours. Based on the information they receive, they form beliefs about the state of the world and take actions accordingly. In equilibrium an agent over-reports, under-reports or truthfully reports to a neighbour depending on the expected action of the concerned neighbour and how central that neighbour is in the network. We also study how an agent's own bias changes to a change in her neighbour's bias. Finally, we explore the conditions under which it is a Nash Equilibrium for all agents to have no bias.

title: Carathéodory-Type Selection and Random Fixed Point Theorems for Discontinuous Correspondences
affiliations: Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata and University of Iowa - Henry B. Tippie College of Business

detail.title: Carathéodory-Type Selection and Random Fixed Point Theorems for Discontinuous Correspondences
detail.abstract: This paper studies Carathéodory-type selection theorems and random fixedpoint theorems motivated by applications in economics and game theory. We establish these results for correspondences that are not required to satisfy standard continuity assumptions, such as lower or upper semicontinuity. Our theorems extend and unify existing selection and fixed-point results and, as special cases, recover the theorems of Kim-Prikry-Yannelis [24]. We further derive new random maximal element theorems and prove the existence of equilibria in large abstract economies, as well as random equilibria, including random Nash and Bayesian equilibria. These findings generalize and refine several classical results due to Browder [8], Fan [11, 12], Nash [30], and others.

title: Quantum Ranking and Selection under Stochastic Constraints
affiliations: Fudan University, Fudan University and East China Normal University (ECNU)

detail.title: Quantum Ranking and Selection under Stochastic Constraints
detail.abstract: With recent advances in quantum information processing, leveraging quantum computing to accelerate classical algorithms has attracted significant attention across multiple research communities. In this paper, we investigate the potential of quantum computing to address the fixed-confidence ranking and selection (R&S) problem under stochastic constraints, a fundamental topic in the simulation community. We begin by defining a quantum oracle for each alternative to characterize the quantum simulation model. Based on this, we derive a query complexity lower bound for any quantum R&S algorithm using quantum hypothesis testing. By comparing this bound to its classical counterpart, we show that a per-alternative quadratic speedup is achievable. Motivated by these results, we propose the first quantum algorithm for constrained R&S, termed QSEAL. QSEAL adopts a sequential elimination framework and uses quantum Monte Carlo methods to construct performance estimators. We establish an upper bound on its query complexity and show that it matches the lower bound under some conditions, which establishes the optimality. For comparison, we also develop a classical algorithm, SEAL, using the same framework and demonstrate that QSEAL attains a substantially lower query complexity than SEAL. Numerical experiments further corroborate this improvement, providing empirical evidence for the query-efficiency advantage of quantum computing in R&S.

title: Labor Market Dynamics Around Childbirth: Evidence from Spanish Administrative Records
affiliations: Universidad del País Vasco, University of Girona and University of Girona

detail.title: Labor Market Dynamics Around Childbirth: Evidence from Spanish Administrative Records
detail.abstract: This paper examines how childbirth affects men’s and women’s labor market dynamics in Spain. Using monthly administrative data, we track individuals across full-time employment, part-time work, registered unemployment, and non-affiliation over a 96-month window around the birth of their first child. A time-varying Markov model captures transitions between these states. Childbirth causes a sharp, persistent decline in women’s full-time employment and a corresponding rise in part-time work, registered unemployment, and non-affiliation, while men’s trajectories remain stable. Lower job-finding probabilities from non-employment states into full-time jobs are the main drivers of these gaps. Compositional factors explain little of the divergence, indicating that institutional and social constraints underlie persistent gender inequalities.

title: Renewable Technologies and Global Spillovers as Drivers of the Energy Transition -A Model-Guided Study and GVAR Empirics (Draft)
affiliations: Curtin University, The New School - Department of Economics and University of Münster

detail.title: Renewable Technologies and Global Spillovers as Drivers of the Energy Transition -A Model-Guided Study and GVAR Empirics (Draft)
detail.abstract: The paper studies to what extent renewable energy technologies and their international spillovers, supported by public policies, are the dominant drivers of the energy transition. We present a model guided-study and some empirics from a Global Vector Autoregressive Regression (GVAR). The model-guided part of the paper elaborates on the global macroeconomic policies and their role in controlling climate risks through mitigation, adaptation and investing in climate-related infrastructure. Hereby the role of the public sector and public finance and their spillover effects are emphasized. Next, we focus on an empirical validation of the climate-economy model using a 30-country Global Vector Autoregressive (GVAR) framework. To proxy the theoretical model we construct a GVAR model with four endogenous variables per country-GDP growth, CO 2 emissions growth, renewable energy share growth and efficiency improvements employing parametric bootstrap methods with 299 replications, we generate 90% confidence intervals for Generalized Impulse Response Functions (GIRFs) across a 20-year horizon. Our results provide qualified support for the theoretical predictions: Renewable energy shocks reduce CO 2 emissions growth, carbon intensity improvement has also a negative effect on emissions and GDP growth has the expected posivite effect on CO 2. The analysis confirms the importance of international spillovers of knowledge, practices and technologies and highlights the complementarity between of renewable energy innovations and efficiency improvements generating effective decarbonization.

title: Involvement of Youth in the Development Programs of Selected Barangays of Caloocan City
affiliations: Independent, Independent and

detail.title: Involvement of Youth in the Development Programs of Selected Barangays of Caloocan City
detail.abstract:
This study examined the extent of youth involvement and influence in the planning, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of Barangay Development Programs, with particular emphasis on Sports and Development initiatives in selected barangays of Caloocan City. Conducted in 2018 in Barangays 174, 175, and 176, the study was anchored on the government’s advocacy for youth participation in nation-building and the national policy of “Sports for All.” It sought to provide an empirical basis for strengthening youth participation and enhancing community-based development programs.

A descriptive research design was employed involving 120 respondents, composed of 30 barangay officials and 90 youth participants. Data were gathered through survey questionnaires and interview guides, and analyzed using percentage distribution and weighted mean. Results indicated that youth development programs were generally aligned with their stated objectives and demonstrated sustainability, although implementation was constrained by variations in financial resources, facilities, and manpower. Youth involvement across the stages of planning, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation was consistently rated as “agree,” signifying meaningful participation and influence, particularly in planning and monitoring processes. However, challenges encountered in program implementation were assessed as “serious,” notably limited budgets, insufficient youth participation, and inadequate facilities.

The study further identified Health and Anti-Drug Abuse as the priority area for program enhancement, followed by education and youth employment initiatives, while sports development ranked lower despite its recognized developmental value. Based on the findings, enhancement and alternative development strategies integrating sports, health promotion, and anti-drug abuse advocacy are proposed to address prevailing community needs. Overall, the study underscores the critical role of structured, adequately resourced, and institutionalized youth participation in ensuring effective and sustainable barangay development programs.

title: Are Private and Public Firms Friends or Foes? Evidence from Millions of Webpages
affiliations: University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business - Finance and Business Economics Department and Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business

detail.title: Are Private and Public Firms Friends or Foes? Evidence from Millions of Webpages

declarations.funderStatement: National Science Foundation grants #1561068 and #1937153, Tuck School of Business, Institute for Outlier Research in Business

detail.abstract: We examine the impact of positive private firm innovation shocks and private firm liquidity shocks on existing public firm peers using an extensive dynamic textual network. We build this textual network using a LLM to analyze millions of internet webpages over time from 2000 to 2021 from the Internet WayBack Machine. We document that state-level shocks to the incentives of private firms to invest in R&D have positive effects on related public firms consistent with product market complementarities. After these innovation shocks to private peers, related public firms increase acquisitions of private firms and have improved profitability, sales growth, competitive positioning, and investments including R&D. In contrast, state-level liquidity shocks, which instead relax financing constraints of private firms located in these states, negatively impact related public firms, consistent with substitution and private firms increasing competitive pressure on public firms. These results indicate a new empirical framework and novel indications of where private firms are either complements or substitutes to larger public firms.

title: Rainchecks & Risk: Climate Shocks, Policy Transitions, and SME Credit Dynamics
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt, Fortune Institute of International Business and Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha (GGSIP) University

detail.title: Rainchecks & Risk: Climate Shocks, Policy Transitions, and SME Credit Dynamics
detail.abstract: Using a panel of 45 countries, 2007-2022, we study how climate risk and the Paris Agreement shape SME bank lending. We combine two-way fixed effects with event-study diagnostics, panel quantile regression, two-step system GMM, local projections with Driscoll-Kraay errors, a structural mediation design, and staggered DiD for Paris ratification. Disasters depress SME credit (approx.-1% on impact in TWFE;-3.6% in 2SGMM), with insignificant placebo leads and persistent post-shock contractions. Effects are negative across the conditional distribution, largest at the median and consistent with a broad supply tightening. Structural conditions matter: higher ND-GAIN Vulnerability lowers lending, while Readiness raises it; part of each effect operates through realised disasters (approx. 11% and 24% mediated). Paris ratification is followed, after a short lag, by a sizeable decline in SME credit that is amplified where vulnerability is high and attenuated where readiness is strong.

detail.title: The Determinants of Green Investments by Institutional Investors: The Role of Government Carbon Mitigation Strategies and Policies

detail.abstract: The increasingly evident shortfall in green financing, particularly from institutional investors, needs to be addressed to advance sustainable development. Currently, the scholarship tends to focus on the effects of regulatory frameworks, market forces and the macroenvironment. However, there is a paucity of research which considers the impact of the interaction of these factors. To address this gap, this study examines whether government capital expenditure influences institutional investors' green investment allocations and whether government carbon mitigation policies moderate this relationship. Using data from the world bank portal, global sovereign wealth funds and the carbon pricing database for the sample period of 2010-2022 across 40 countries, this study uses OLS, GLS and Quantile regressions to address the research questions and System Dynamic GMM regression is used for robustness checks. Additionally, the Heckman test is used to test whether sample selection bias exists. The findings from Quantile regression indicate that an increase in government funding influences institutional investors' green investments, within the middle and upper quantiles. While the results obtained from the GLS estimation for the full sample suggest that government investments may be insufficient on their own; when combined with carbon policies and carbon laws, institutional investors are persuaded or discouraged to undertake green investments. This study has policy implications as it demonstrates how institutional investors respond to government actions. When green investments are supported by long-term policy frameworks and fiscal spending, they become more appealing and align with fiduciary obligations. This study also covers SDGs 9, 12 and 13.

title: The Most Stringent Environmental Regulation and Industrial Restructuring in China
affiliations: , Tsinghua University and Nanyang Technological University

detail.title: The Most Stringent Environmental Regulation and Industrial Restructuring in China
detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of the most stringent environmental regulation ever implemented in China, the 2013 Air Pollution Prevention and Control Action Plan (the Plan), on firm dynamics in both local and nonlocal domestic markets. Exploiting a comprehensive firm registration database covering all firms in mainland China from 2008 to 2017, and combining a difference-indifference-indifference design, we document substantial impacts of the Plan on the focal regulated "two high" sectors (high energy-consuming and highpolluting). The Plan significantly reduces firm entry into local markets but has little effect on firm exit, with stronger impacts for micro-sized and private firms and for eastern coastal cities. We find that the regulatory effects spill over along the production network to non-"two high" manufacturing, upstream, and downstream sectors. The Plan stimulates innovation among incumbent "two high" firms, partially accounting for the observed findings. Furthermore, spatially uneven regulatory stringency across cities leads to a westward relocation of pollution-intensive industries, primarily driven by the coal-fired power generation sector. This paper demonstrates that stringent environmental regulation in a transitioning economy can fundamentally reshape the structure of pollutionintensive industries.

title: What Is My Home Worth?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia

detail.title: What Is My Home Worth?

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Philadelphia Working Paper No. 25-40
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Economic models often assume that agents always know the market value of their assets. We use residential property tax assessment as a laboratory to test this assumption for housing. We first show that assessed market value (AMV) is a noisy proxy for transaction-based market value (TMV). Innovations in AMV are less volatile than, are weakly correlated with, and lag innovations in TMV. An AMV-based, national-level house price index has shallower troughs and shorter peaks than its TMV-based counterpart. We merge in anonymized credit bureau data to test whether homeowners use AMVs, as signals of housing wealth, to make consumption decisions. Using local mass reassessments as an instrument, we find that AMV changes causally affect the likelihood that households take out a new home equity line of credit (HELOC) with a similar economic magnitude as TMV changes. A partial equilibrium calibration exercise suggests that innovations in AMV can explain approximately 1% of annual HELOC origination. Overall, our results suggest that homeowners do not fully know the value of their homes.
